description: We are Team SkyBound, a multidisciplinary engineering and science team  with expertise in Computer Science, Data Engineering, and Remote Sensing. Our core interests focus on solving the 2026 satellite transition crisis by building machine learning harmonization pipelines, spatiotemporal grid clustering, and bias-correction models that bridge MODIS and VIIRS thermal detections to prevent climate observation blackouts.
summary: SkyBound is a web app that harmonises 26 years of NASA FIRMS fire detections from MODIS (2000–2025) and VIIRS (2012–2026) into one burn calendar for South Asia. We built a calibration layer that scales MODIS-era counts to the VIIRS scale using per-country factors fitted on 2012–2019 overlap days and tested on 2020–2025. This removes the sensor step that otherwise makes 2013 look like an extreme fire year. Users can pick a country and date to see whether activity is above its seasonal norm, view a year-by-month calendar, and export daily analytics and hotspots as CSV. This supports early warning responders, firefighters, and land managers, who need a consistent record to judge whether current burning is unusual. Next steps are region selection, date ranges, and next-week forecasts.
details:
Before the details, a correction. Earlier I said the app had no CSV download, no date range, and no region selection. Your screenshots show all three in the Streamlit app: "Download Search Hotspots CSV", "Download 2000–2026 Daily Analytics CSV", a Search Start/End Date picker, and a "Custom Lat/Lon" option. So those gaps were overstated. The screenshots also show the Streamlit app does not yet have the calibrated mode, only Harmonised and Raw.

What it does

SkyBound is a web app for burn monitoring in South Asia. It combines NASA FIRMS fire detections from MODIS (2000 onward) and VIIRS (2012 onward) into one record on a 5.5 km grid. Users pick a country or enter coordinates, choose a date range, and see:

  • A map of active fire cells and next-7-day spread risk.
  • A year-by-month calendar of burning from 2000 to 2026.
  • An anomaly check that compares a chosen day with its seasonal baseline (±7 days, 2000–2025).
  • Daily analytics and hotspot lists as CSV downloads.

The calibration layer, which I added, scales MODIS-era counts to the VIIRS scale. Factors are fitted per country on 2012–2019 overlap days and tested on 2020–2025. With calibration, the 2013 India "extreme burning" result becomes "within normal range", so the 2012 sensor change is no longer mistaken for a fire surge.

Benefits

  • One consistent record across two sensors, so comparisons across years are fair.
  • Quick answers to "is this unusual for this place and time of year?"
  • Free, public data sources, so the tool can be reused by other agencies.

Intended impact

The main users are early-warning responders, firefighters, and land managers. The aim is to help them spot unusual burning sooner and plan response. The impact is not yet measured: we have no field trial or user study, so this should be described as a potential benefit.

Tools and software

  • Python, with pandas, NumPy, and pyarrow for data processing and Parquet storage.
  • FastAPI for the backend API.
  • Streamlit and Plotly for the interactive dashboard.
  • JavaScript, HTML, and CSS for the static web version.
  • pytest for tests.
  • NASA FIRMS MODIS C6.1 and VIIRS 375 m data.

Creativity

  • Calibrating two sensors per country and testing the fit on held-out years, rather than relying on a correlation score.
  • Confidence tiers that show how reliable each country's calibration is.
  • A warning on the anomaly check when its baseline mixes sensor eras.
  • Combining the anomaly check, calendar, and spread-risk map in one view.

Factors we considered

  • Sensor continuity: MODIS is ending while VIIRS is starting, so the record has to bridge both.
  • Data reliability: low-overlap countries like the Maldives are left uncalibrated, and Afghanistan and Bhutan are flagged as low confidence.
  • Accessibility: a colour ramp chosen for readability.
  • Honest reporting: the dashboard reports correlation and calibration error rather than a single headline number.

Open issues to resolve before submission

  • The calibrated mode isn't in the Streamlit app yet.
  • The 2026 MODIS-to-VIIRS ratio of 8.37 is unexplained.
  • The "Suomi-NPP end-of-delivery on 2 November 2026" statement in the app is still unverified.
  • The calibration was applied to the existing fixture rather than regenerated from raw data.
